newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatians to prefer strong rule to more democracy.
newsitem.headline: Croatians to prefer strong rule to more democracy.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman seems certain to win reelection on Sunday as opinion polls show Croatians preferring the 75-year-old "Father of the Nation's" firm hand to promises of more democracy.
"Croatia is a young democracy and it is normal that it needs a strongman," said Ana Ferle, a scientist from Zagreb. "Without him, there would be a reign of anarchy."
Tudjman's two rivals, Vlado Gotovac of the Social Liberal party and Zdravko Tomac of the Social Democrats, have made much of his autocratic rule and they promise to reduce presidential powers.
But as the campaigning ended on Saturday for 24 hours of reflection before the vote, Tudjman looked set to sweep to outright victory.
Tudjman, who led Croatia to independence from communist Yugoslavia in 1991, is still hugely popular despite growing criticism, both at home and abroad, of his autocratic rule.
A survey published in the independent weekly Nacional showed one-third of Croatians even think he should be made president for life.

"I waited for 50 years for a man who would create an independent Croatia," said 57-year-old Anton, a lawyer. "I was convinced I would not live to see it and that communism would last for another 300 years."
"There is not a single politician on the horizon who is up to Tudjman's knees," Ferle said.
The president is reported to be suffering from cancer and might not live out another five-year term in office.
While Gotovac, a poet and inspired orator, appeals to intellectuals and the young, Tomac, a leader of reformed communists, underscores his care for poverty-stricken workers and pensioners.

Both promise to reduce the powers of the president and ruling Croatian Democratic Union party (HDZ) and lavish perks enjoyed by the establishment. They say Croatia is run by an oligarchy of 200 wealthy, politically-connected families.

"Nothing will depend on one man and one signature...you should not need HDZ passes for everything you do," Gotovac said at a rally in Zagreb. "We want a country where citizens will feel like decision-makers."
"The Croatian state will not perish after Tudjman is gone," Tomac said. "I fight for a democratic alternative. If I am president I will live like you, walk with you and be with you."
Polls give each of them each some 15 percent of votes, not even enough to force Tudjman into second round.

"I'd vote for Tudjman only if I got drunk," said one opposition supporter, 74-year-old pensioner Rozika. "He and his party have pockets deep as peasants' wells and those wells are never full and can always take more water."
"I give support to Tomac's ideas, which is to protect the poor, to change Croatia so people can smile again and not cry and look in garbage containers for food," said Margareta, 60.
But in most cases, their messages do not seem to have a widespread appeal.
"The problem is most people have no idea what democracy really is...There has never been a real democracy or civic rights here," said 35-year-old Jadranka, a professor.
"I also think people are generally afraid of change. It is like with a boyfriend - you keep dating him because you fear change although your relationship may be terrible."
Many voters also feel that both opposition candidates lack political charisma.
"Gotovac doesn't belong to politics, he should go back to his poetry and philosophy and Tomac is a political hack," said Josko Pavkovic, 19, a law student.
Tomac also has to fight against the communist legacy of his party, often portrayed by the state media and the HDZ as the successor to the Yugoslav communist party which ruled Croatia for 50 years.
